**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The cursor blinks on the screen like a tiny, impatient heart. *Write something*, it seems to say. *Anything.* And so I do.

A thousand words is both a vast expanse and a suffocating box. It’s enough to build a world, to sketch a life, to unravel a thought until it frays at the edges. But it’s also a limit—a boundary that whispers, *You can’t say everything.* So I won’t. I’ll say some things. Small things. True things. Maybe even beautiful ones.

The morning light slants through my window, gold and slow, like honey poured from a great height. Outside, a pigeon coos, and I wonder if it’s the same one that’s been perched on my fire escape for weeks. Does it recognize me? Do I recognize it? We’re both creatures of habit, after all. It pecks at crumbs I don’t remember dropping. I type words I don’t always mean to say.

There’s a coffee mug beside me, half-full, long cold. The dregs at the bottom are bitter, like the last thoughts of the day. I should’ve finished it when it was hot. I should’ve done a lot of things.

Memory is a strange thing. It’s not a filing cabinet, neat and ordered. It’s more like a junk drawer—full of ticket stubs, old keys, a single mitten, the scent of rain on pavement in a city you haven’t lived in for years. Pull one thread, and the whole thing might unravel. Or maybe nothing happens. Maybe the thread just dangles there, useless.

I think about the people who’ve passed through my life like comets—bright, brief, leaving a trail of light that lingers long after they’re gone. There was the man at the bus stop who told me, unprompted, that his wife had died, and then smiled like he’d just shared a secret. There was the child on the subway who pressed a dandelion into my palm and said, *For you, because you look sad.* (I wasn’t sad. But maybe I was.)

Small kindnesses. Tiny miracles. The world is full of them, if you’re paying attention.

And then there are the other things—the way a city can feel like a prison of noise and hurry, how loneliness isn’t the absence of people but the absence of being seen. How sometimes, the heaviest silence isn’t between two people, but inside your own head.

I once read that a blue whale’s heart beats so loudly it can be heard from two miles away. Imagine that—an organ so vast its rhythm is a pulse for the ocean. What must it be like to carry something so immense inside you? Do whales know the weight of their own hearts? Or do they just swim, unaware, until one day they surface, gasping, and realize the sky is still there, vast and indifferent and beautiful?

We’re all whales, in a way. Carrying things we don’t speak of. Love. Grief. The quiet ache of wanting to mean something in a universe that doesn’t always notice.

But then there’s this: the act of writing. Of stringing words together like beads, hoping they’ll hold when the string frays. It’s a kind of faith, really—the belief that if you shape the chaos just right, someone, somewhere, will understand. That you’re not alone.

The pigeon is gone now. The light has shifted. The coffee is stone cold. And the cursor still blinks.

A thousand words. I’ve used some of them. Not all. That’s okay. The rest can wait.

They’re patient.
The page is infinite.
